newsitem.title: USA: Browner says will not be swayed from air proposal.
newsitem.headline: Browner says will not be swayed from air proposal.

text.p: The Clinton administration's top environmental regulator said Friday she intends to stick with a plan to tighten air quality standards that has raised a furore among industry groups.

"Let me say this -- when it comes to protecting our kids, I will not be swayed. If the science shows that we have to do more to ensure that our kids are safe from pollution, then that is precisely what we will do," Carol Browner, Environmental Protection Agency administrator, said at a conference on children's health.
The Clinton administration proposed setting stricter standards against ground-level ozone, which creates smog, and against microscopic airborne particles, or soot, that can lodge deep in lungs.
"We're proposing to strengthen national air quality standards for smog and soot to a level that will protect millions more children from the harmful effects of these pollutants," Browner said.

The proposal, considered the EPA's most significant in recent years, also was the subject of a debate Friday held by the League of Women Voters and attended by a number of staffers of members of Congress who are evaluating the issue.

The debated pitted speakers for Citizens for a Sound Economy, who said the EPA proposal would be too costly to implement, against speakers for the Sierra Club, who said the standards would prolong thousands of lives and ease millions of cases of respiratory illness.
"The bottom line is this is a choice between kids' health and corporate profits," said Ron White, deputy director of the American Lung Association and one of the Sierra Club's debaters.

But Republican Representative Thomas Coburn of Oklahoma, speaking for the business group, said, "We should spend the first dollar that gives us the greatest help." He said money spent to implement these standards could be better spent on research on cancer or genetics.

Boyden Gray, White House counsel in the Bush administration and another speaker for the business group, said air quality was improving under existing regulations and the EPA ought to take more time to research the need for new standards.
"They do make mistakes," he said of the agency.
